questions.title: How can the Board find 'legal identity' between credit card services and general banking services when the parties explicitly state they do not compete directly?
questions.question_body: I am struggling with the Board's analysis of the second DuPont factor regarding the similarity of goods/services. The opinion states that CC Serve partners with banks to issue cards but doesn't offer banking services itself, while Apex is a bank offering loans and deposits but *no* credit cards. Yet, the Board concluded their services are 'legally identical, in part' simply because dictionary definitions of 'banking' encompass issuing credit cards. How does the court reconcile this broad dictionary definition approach with the practical reality that these are distinct business models? Is this a new trend where functional overlaps in definitions trump actual market competition?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit vacate the Sixth DuPont Factor analysis based on a definitional inconsistency rather than just reviewing for substantial evidence?
questions.question_body: In section III.B, the court vacates the Board's finding on the sixth factor (third-party marks). My confusion lies in why this wasn't just a 'substantial evidence' issue. The Board found only 9 similar marks for 'credit card services,' which wasn't enough to prove weakness. However, Apex wanted to include 42 other marks involving broader financial services. The court says restricting the universe was a legal error because it contradicted their own finding in Factor Two (that services are highly similar). Why does defining 'similar goods' differently across different DuPont factors constitute reversible legal error? Shouldn't the Board have discretion to define the relevant market narrowly for each specific factor?

questions.title: What is the procedural mechanism for remanding a trademark case when one factor's re-evaluation logically necessitates changing another unrelated factor?
questions.question_body: The court vacated both Factor Six and Factor One (similarity of marks). I understand why Factor Six needed a redo if we expand the pool of third-party marks (as per my previous question), but why did that automatically force a re-examination of Factor One? The opinion states: 'reconsideration of the sixth DuPont factor may result in a different determination of the mark’s commercial strength... and affect the overall commercial impression.' Doesn't commercial strength usually feed into distinctiveness or fame, whereas commercial impression is about visual/phonetic similarity? I'm trying to understand if there is an inherent link between 'market crowding' (Factor Six) and how consumers perceive two specific words ('Aspire' vs 'Aspire Bank') that makes them inseparable on remand.

questions.title: Does this ruling imply that once courts find services are 'highly similar,' they must treat all subsequent DuPont factors as having an expanded scope automatically?
questions.question_body: The core holding seems to hinge on consistency: since Factor Two said services are highly similar, Factor Six couldn't limit its search to just credit cards. Does this create a rigid rule where finding similarity in Factor Two locks in a broad interpretation for all other factors? If so, how does this interact with cases where courts typically analyze each DuPont factor somewhat independently based on its specific evidentiary record? Am I missing nuance here regarding whether this is about logical consistency or something deeper about how trademark rights scale with service breadth?

questions.title: If Apex didn't actually offer credit cards yet (intent-to-use), does that change how we evaluate likelihood of confusion compared to actual concurrent use?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions Apex filed an intent-to-use application and planned to launch later, while CC Serve had active registrations since 1996. Usually, likelihood of confusion looks at current market conditions. Since Apex hadn't started selling yet during most of this timeline, does that weaken or strengthen their argument against confusion? Or does it matter at all given that Lanham Act Section 2(d) prohibits registration even before use if confusion is likely upon launch? I'm confused about how temporal proximity plays into these specific du Pont analyses when one party hasn't entered the market.
